Today's TL;DRRegimeRISK-OFF
A global risk-off wave is underway as renewed US-Iran hostilities and tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz send oil prices surging, while hawkish central-bank repricing—sparked by Fed Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole speech and euro-zone inflation hitting a near-three-year high—drives bond yields to multi-year highs. Safe-haven flows strengthen the dollar and pressure equities, though AI-infrastructure earnings (Dell, Palo Alto Networks) and chip-boom momentum in Asia provide pockets of resilience. The combination of energy-driven inflation fears and tightening monetary policy creates a stagflationary backdrop, with September seasonality and geopolitical uncertainty compounding the bearish tone.

AI Infrastructure Capex SurgeAI 基建资本开支激增
×10 · 43 steps
Hyperscaler and sovereign AI capex is surging, with top 4 CSPs capex up 87% YoY in 2Q26 and US hyperscaler capex projected at $940bn. AI and technology investment remains fundamentally strong despite macro headwinds. Compute supply growth continues to lag demand for AI services, with MiniMax's training utilization reaching 97% in 1H26 and Goldman Sachs expecting the imbalance to persist through 2028; Morgan Stanley estimates SpaceX's $100bn Starbase LA facility represents only 2% of total capex given AI spending scale, funded partly by ~$80bn/yr net debt issuance.

China domestic demand weakness中国国内需求疲软
×7 · 30 steps
China's domestic demand remains soft with consumer caution weighing on e-commerce (Kuaishou), catering softness (Foshan Haitian), a passenger vehicle down cycle with sales declining from 24mn to below 20mn units by 2028E (GAC), and broad macro weakness with manufacturing PMI at 49.8 and non-manufacturing at 49.0. Chinese consumer demand remains persistently weak, with retail sales growth stagnating at 0-1% YoY and industrial production capacity utilization at 73% in 2Q26. Despite Politburo and State Council pledges, these indicators confirm the continued weakness.

US-Iran conflict is driving volatility in energy prices and supply chains. Strait of Hormuz disruptions reduced crude exports from ~15 mb/d to ~6 mb/d. Brent at ~$94/bbl despite disruption absorbed by stockpiling and supplier diversification. Ongoing Middle East disruptions continue to propagate globally: limited LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz keep 3Q26 US-to-Asia net gas spreads near $14.80/mmbtu and 4Q26-4Q27 strip spreads up ~40%, while Middle East logistics disruptions also drive MLCC sales shortfalls and a likely decline in Taiyo Yuden's 1.72 book-to-bill ratio.

×4 · 14 steps
Rising long-term Treasury yields reflect macro (cyclical resilience, AI capex optimism, fiscal pressures) rather than supply indigestion. US federal debt has surged to ~$40T (doubled in ten years), with deficits remaining near $2tn per year. Goldman Sachs notes that long-end buybacks offset about 30% of gross 20y and 30y issuance, stabilizing the long-end.   1. 1
    Premise

  2. 2
    Mechanism
    Since US public debt surpassed $31 trillion in October 2022, the subsequent $9 trillion increase coincided with only 13bp of tightening in 10y SOFR swap spreads but 4bp of widening in 30y swap spreads; the stock of debt rose but its relative price did not move uniformly.
    dd37bbd5427e·《A 40 Trillion Dollar Distraction》·2026-08-30
  3. 3
    Mechanism

    ecf3b849fe14·《$40T of Debt: Brake or Break?》·2026-08-25

    Conclusion

J.P. Morgan4 steps
  1. 1
    Premise
    JPMorgan views Alibaba's sell-off as too large relative to the actual shareholder cost: only 0.3% of the share-price move is the arithmetic of issuing at a discount, while the abnormal repricing of existing holders of about US$19bn is roughly twice the US$10.3bn cash raised; the more accurate conclusion from the placement is narrower, namely that Alibaba's AI investment cycle is likely longer than expected but underlying compute economics remain attractive and the three CSPs in coverage have very different funding risks.
    04b97ac550d1·《Who Pays for the AI Build?》·2026-08-27
  2. 2
    Mechanism
    JPMorgan's vintage model gives a 22% project IRR against a cost of capital near 10%, a 2.9-year payback and RMB36 NPV per RMB100 of capex at the 100% infrastructure mix and RMB22 NPV at the 60% base mix, reconciling management's sub-three-year payback and 13%+ blended ROIC.
    04b97ac550d1·《Who Pays for the AI Build?》·2026-08-27
  3. 3
    Mechanism
    Returns cannot simply be scaled with capex: 80% mature utilization with 10% lower pricing earns only about 11% project IRR, and 70% utilization with 20% lower pricing earns about 3%, which is how a bigger program becomes a worse one and why RMB270bn is a risk case rather than upside.
    04b97ac550d1·《Who Pays for the AI Build?》·2026-08-27
  4. 4
    Conclusion
    EPS turns accretive from year two if at least 80% of proceeds become infrastructure but stays modestly dilutive at the 60% base mix (-2.0% in FY27E, -0.5% in FY28E), and year-three accretion requires a mature ROIC of roughly 15% when proceeds are substantially deployed.
    04b97ac550d1·《Who Pays for the AI Build?》·2026-08-27

J.P. Morgan4 steps
  1. 1
    Premise
    JPMorgan views Alibaba's sell-off as too large relative to the actual shareholder cost: only 0.3% of the share-price move is the arithmetic of issuing at a discount, while the abnormal repricing of existing holders of about US$19bn is roughly twice the US$10.3bn cash raised; the more accurate conclusion from the placement is narrower, namely that Alibaba's AI investment cycle is likely longer than expected but underlying compute economics remain attractive and the three CSPs in coverage have very different funding risks.
    04b97ac550d1·《Who Pays for the AI Build?》·2026-08-27
  2. 2
    Mechanism
    JPMorgan's vintage model gives a 22% project IRR against a cost of capital near 10%, a 2.9-year payback and RMB36 NPV per RMB100 of capex at the 100% infrastructure mix and RMB22 NPV at the 60% base mix, reconciling management's sub-three-year payback and 13%+ blended ROIC.
    04b97ac550d1·《Who Pays for the AI Build?》·2026-08-27
  3. 3
    Mechanism
    Returns cannot simply be scaled with capex: 80% mature utilization with 10% lower pricing earns only about 11% project IRR, and 70% utilization with 20% lower pricing earns about 3%, which is how a bigger program becomes a worse one and why RMB270bn is a risk case rather than upside.
    04b97ac550d1·《Who Pays for the AI Build?》·2026-08-27
  4. 4
    Conclusion
    EPS turns accretive from year two if at least 80% of proceeds become infrastructure but stays modestly dilutive at the 60% base mix (-2.0% in FY27E, -0.5% in FY28E), and year-three accretion requires a mature ROIC of roughly 15% when proceeds are substantially deployed.
    04b97ac550d1·《Who Pays for the AI Build?》·2026-08-27

Watching for the pre-crash 'hot sector, narrow rally' pattern

XBI 63-day excess return +27.5pp (99th percentile of 10 years) · Market breadth at the 92nd percentile (broad participation) · XBI +25.8% above its 200-day MA (94th percentile)
Thresholds calibrated on a single event — the 2026-06/07 semiconductor selloff (n=1)
Trigger rule details
The three observed quantities
Sector relative strength = how far a sector's return has beaten the broad market's over the trailing quarter (a price proxy for crowding)
Market breadth = how many stocks participate in the rally (equal-weight index underperforming cap-weight = narrowing breadth)
% above 200-day MA = how far price sits above its own 200-day moving average (the standard BIAS technical indicator)
How the light is decided
🔴 Red: hottest sector's relative strength enters the top 5% of 10 years (≥95) AND market breadth narrows into the top 10% (≥90) — both must hold
🟡 Amber: relative strength ≥95 but breadth only to ≥60; or either relative strength or 200-day bias enters the top 1% (≥99)
🟢 Green: everything else
Once red has fired, it doesn't snap straight back to green: it must exit the top 20% (relative strength) or the top 60% (breadth) before returning to green, resting on amber in between (anti-flicker)
Any missing data shows “No data” — it never defaults to green
